issues.legal_issue: A court may withdraw an interim arrangement allowing a developer to complete stalled housing projects when the developer fails to comply with the arrangement and its undertakings, and may place completion work in other hands to protect home buyers.
material_facts: The developer had agreed to complete the projects with co-developers and to deposit money in an escrow account, but did not deposit the required amount or carry out the promised work.
The developer repeatedly changed its position before the Court, and a co-developer later withdrew from the arrangement.
The Court found the developer’s conduct unfair and found that it had violated the Court’s orders.
The Court appointed a public construction corporation to study and undertake completion of the projects.
issues.conclusion: The Court recalled its earlier order entrusting completion to the developer and co-developers and directed the public construction corporation to study the projects and submit a completion proposal.
issues.legal_principle: In the exercise of its jurisdiction in proceedings brought to protect home buyers, the Court treated the developer’s failure to honour the arrangement and its undertakings, together with its shifting positions and non-compliance, as grounds to recall the interim arrangement and make a different completion arrangement. Article 32 is the stated basis for the petitions; no earlier case is relied on for this ruling.

rule.if: housing_project_proceeding and (developer_failed_to_perform_completion_commitments or developer_repeatedly_changed_its_position) and court_order_noncompliance and home_buyers_face_uncompleted_homes

predicates.housing_project_proceeding: The proceeding concerns housing projects in which home buyers have not received completed homes.
predicates.developer_failed_to_perform_completion_c: The developer did not carry out the completion work it had undertaken to perform.
predicates.developer_repeatedly_changed_its_positio: The developer presented shifting positions about how the projects would be completed.
predicates.court_order_noncompliance: The developer failed to comply with directions made by the Court.
predicates.home_buyers_face_uncompleted_homes: Home buyers remained without the homes promised to them because the projects were incomplete.
predicates.promoter_completion_authority_is_withdra: The developer is no longer entrusted with completing the projects under the earlier arrangement.

issues.definition: When a housing-project proceeding involves uncompleted homes, non-compliance with court orders, and failure to perform completion commitments or shifting positions by the developer, the developer’s authority under the completion arrangement is withdrawn.

issues.legal_issue: The Court may preserve the assets and accounts of a developer and its directors when the record prima facie shows that money collected for housing projects was diverted.
material_facts: The developer admitted that substantial sums collected for certain projects had been transferred to other projects.
The developer did not comply with the Court’s direction to deposit money in an escrow account.
The Court found a prima facie basis to conclude that money paid by buyers for particular projects could not be diverted before those projects were completed.
The Court directed that the companies’ and directors’ bank accounts be frozen and their properties attached, while stating that it was not expressing a final opinion on criminal breach of trust.
issues.conclusion: The Court ordered interim freezing of the companies’ and directors’ bank accounts and attachment of the relevant properties, restricting dealings without the Court’s permission.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the prima facie diversion of funds provided for specified housing projects as a basis for interim asset-preservation directions to protect home buyers and secure the subject matter of the proceedings. The Court referred to Article 32 as the basis for the petitions and described the suspected diversion as potentially amounting to criminal breach of trust, but made no final determination. No earlier case is relied on for this interim ruling.

rule.if: housing_project_proceeding and buyers_paid_for_specific_projects and project_funds_were_diverted and assets_may_be_needed_to_protect_buyers

predicates.housing_project_proceeding: The proceeding concerns housing projects for which buyers paid money but did not receive completed homes.
predicates.buyers_paid_for_specific_projects: Home buyers paid money for the completion of identified housing projects.
predicates.project_funds_were_diverted: Money collected for those projects was transferred or used elsewhere before the projects were completed.
predicates.assets_may_be_needed_to_protect_buyers: The assets or accounts may be required to safeguard buyers’ interests in the proceeding.
predicates.related_accounts_and_assets_are_preserve: The relevant accounts and assets cannot be dealt with freely and remain subject to the Court’s control.

issues.definition: When buyers have paid for specific housing projects and their funds have been diverted, the related accounts and assets are preserved under court control if that preservation may protect the buyers.

issues.legal_issue: A government committee may not deal with a matter already before the Supreme Court in a way that affects the Court’s existing orders without first obtaining the Court’s permission.
material_facts: The Court had made an order concerning completion of the housing projects and remained seized of the matter.
A government committee held a meeting concerning the same developer and projects without seeking the Court’s permission.
The Court considered that the committee’s action could render its existing order ineffective.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the committee needed the Court’s express permission before taking up the matter and directed relevant officials to explain their actions.
issues.legal_principle: Where the Court is seized of a matter and has made orders governing it, a separate committee should obtain the Court’s express permission before acting on that matter in a way that may undermine those orders. No statutory provision or earlier case is cited for this ruling.

rule.if: supreme_court_proceeding_is_pending and court_has_made_orders_on_the_matter and outside_committee_acts_on_the_same_matter_without_permission and its_action_may_undermine_court_orders

predicates.supreme_court_proceeding_is_pending: A proceeding about the matter remains pending before the Supreme Court.
predicates.court_has_made_orders_on_the_matter: The Court has already made orders governing the matter.
predicates.outside_committee_acts_on_the_same_matte: A committee outside the Court acts on the matter without first obtaining the Court’s permission.
predicates.its_action_may_undermine_court_orders: The committee’s action may make the Court’s existing orders ineffective.
predicates.outside_committee_must_obtain_court_perm: The committee must obtain the Court’s permission before acting on the matter.

issues.definition: When a matter is pending before the Supreme Court, the Court has made orders on it, and an outside committee acts without permission in a way that may undermine those orders, the committee must obtain the Court’s permission before acting.

issues.legal_issue: An order protecting construction work from coercive action does not prevent police from investigating suspected criminal conduct connected with the housing projects.
material_facts: The Court had earlier stated that no coercive action should be taken against buildings where completion work was proceeding under its orders.
The developer used that statement in a manner that raised concern that it was being treated as a bar to police investigation.
The Court clarified that the earlier statement did not restrict investigation of criminal cases or registered complaints.

The Court permitted the police to investigate the projects and the roles of the developer’s directors, finance officer, and statutory auditor, and stated that its orders did not prevent the police from arresting or taking other directors into custody.
issues.conclusion: The Court clarified that its project-completion orders did not bar police investigation and permitted investigation of the suspected conduct and the relevant individuals’ roles.
issues.legal_principle: A direction against coercive action concerning buildings where court-supervised completion work is ongoing is confined to that purpose and does not bar criminal investigation. The Court referred to the distinction between protection of the construction work and investigation of criminal cases; no statutory provision or earlier case is relied on for this ruling.

predicates.housing_project_proceeding: The proceeding concerns housing projects whose construction is being addressed by the Court.
predicates.court_order_protects_ongoing_constructio: The Court has directed that coercive action not be taken against buildings where court-supervised completion work is ongoing.
predicates.police_are_investigating_suspected_crimi: The police are investigating suspected criminal conduct connected with the projects.
predicates.construction_protection_order_does_not_b: The construction-protection order does not prevent the police from investigating suspected criminal conduct.

issues.definition: When the Court protects ongoing construction in a housing-project proceeding and police are investigating suspected criminal conduct connected with the projects, that protection does not bar the investigation.
